Reading arctan: find the ratio in the tan θ column and read the angle on the left — tan θ = 1 ⇒ θ = 45°. A gradient with $G_x = G_y$ therefore points at 45°. Every direction you are asked to name is one of the rows above; if your ratio is not in the tan θ column, re-check the arithmetic rather than reaching for a calculator.

† forward only. tan repeats every 180°, but arctan answers only within −90° to 90°: tan 180° = 0 is true, yet arctan(0) = 0°, not 180°. Read backwards only from the 0°–90° rows.

Negative ratios: arctan(−x) = −arctan(x), so arctan(−1) = −45°.

Pythagorean triples — these give the magnitude $\sqrt{G_x^2+G_y^2}$ as a whole number, not an angle: 3-4-5 · 5-12-13 · 6-8-10 · 8-15-17 · 7-24-25 · 20-21-29 — and any multiple, e.g. 24-32-40. Magnitude and direction are separate questions; read the direction from the tan θ column above.

Square roots: √2 ≈ 1.414 · √3 ≈ 1.732 · √5 ≈ 2.236 · √8 ≈ 2.828 · √32 ≈ 5.657

Powers of two (bit depth, pyramid levels): $2^4 = 16$ · $2^6 = 64$ · $2^8 = 256$ · $2^{10} = 1024$ · $2^{24} = 16{,}777{,}216$ · log₂ 8 = 3 · log₂ 16 = 4 · log₂ 256 = 8

Session 2 · Image Formation & Sensing

A · Pinhole & perspective

Slides for this part →
001⭐Perspective projection1 pts · ~2 min
A camera with focal length $f = 28\text{ mm}$ photographs a person $X = 1.75\text{ m}$ tall standing $Z = 7\text{ m}$ away. How tall is the person on the image plane?
Show solution
Step 1: use $x = f\,\dfrac{X}{Z}$. The metres in $X/Z$ cancel, so $x$ comes out in millimetres, like $f$.
    $x = 28 \times \dfrac{1.75}{7} = 28 \times 0.25 = 7$
→ the person is 7 mm tall on the image plane [1]
Answer: $x = 7\text{ mm}$
Common mistake: mixing units — keep $f$ in mm and both $X$ and $Z$ in m.
002⭐⭐Solving for the distance3 pts · ~5 min
A tree $X = 12\text{ m}$ tall appears $x = 6\text{ mm}$ tall through a lens with $f = 50\text{ mm}$. (a) How far away is the tree? (b) You walk until you are $25\text{ m}$ from the tree. How tall is it on the image now?
Show solution
(a) Step 1: rearrange $x = f\,\dfrac{X}{Z}$ into $Z = \dfrac{fX}{x}$. The mm of $f$ and $x$ cancel; $Z$ is in metres.
    $Z = \dfrac{50 \times 12}{6} = \dfrac{600}{6} = 100$
→ the tree is 100 m away [1.5]
(b) Step 1: same formula with $Z = 25\text{ m}$
    $x = 50 \times \dfrac{12}{25} = \dfrac{600}{25} = 24$
→ 24 mm: four times closer, four times taller [1.5]
Answer: (a) $Z = 100\text{ m}$ · (b) $x = 24\text{ mm}$
003⭐⭐Depth is lost2 pts · ~4 min
A camera with $f = 40\text{ mm}$ sees a post $2\text{ m}$ tall at $8\text{ m}$. (a) How tall is the post on the image? (b) A tower $5\text{ m}$ tall would give exactly the same image. How far away would it have to stand?
Show solution
(a) Step 1: $x = f\,\dfrac{X}{Z} = 40 \times \dfrac{2}{8} = 10$
→ 10 mm [1]
(b) Step 1: the image only depends on the ratio $X/Z$, so the tower needs the same ratio $\dfrac{2}{8} = \dfrac{1}{4}$
    $\dfrac{5}{Z} = \dfrac{1}{4} \;\Rightarrow\; Z = 20$
→ 20 m away — from the image alone you cannot tell the post from the tower [1]
Answer: (a) $10\text{ mm}$ · (b) $Z = 20\text{ m}$
004⭐Pinhole size: light and blur2 pts · ~3 min
A pinhole camera's hole is widened from $0.5\text{ mm}$ to $1.5\text{ mm}$ across. (a) How many times more light comes in? (b) What happens to the blur of each scene point?
Show solution
(a) Step 1: light grows with the hole's area, which grows with the square of its width
    $\left(\dfrac{1.5}{0.5}\right)^2 = 3^2 = 9$
→ 9 times more light [1]
(b) Step 1: each scene point now lands as a disc about as wide as the hole — 3 times wider — so the picture is 3 times blurrier [1]
Answer: (a) $\times 9$ light · (b) blur discs $3\times$ wider
Common mistake: answering $\times 3$ for (a) — light follows the area, not the width.
005⭐⭐⭐Why parallel lines meet3 pts · ~5 min
Two straight rails are $1.5\text{ m}$ apart. A camera with $f = 20\text{ mm}$ looks along them. (a) How far apart are the rails on the image where they are $10\text{ m}$ away? (b) Where they are $100\text{ m}$ away? (c) Use your answers to explain why the rails meet at a point in the photo.
Show solution
(a) Step 1: the gap is an object of size $X = 1.5\text{ m}$, so $x = f\,\dfrac{X}{Z} = 20 \times \dfrac{1.5}{10} = 3$
→ 3 mm [1]
(b) Step 1: $x = 20 \times \dfrac{1.5}{100} = 0.3$
→ 0.3 mm [1]
(c) Step 1: the gap on the image is $f \cdot 1.5 / Z$. As $Z$ grows without limit the gap shrinks toward 0, so far away both rails land on the same point — the vanishing point [1]
Answer: (a) $3\text{ mm}$ · (b) $0.3\text{ mm}$ · (c) the gap $\to 0$ as $Z \to \infty$

B · Lenses

Slides for this part →
006⭐Field of view2 pts · ~3 min
A sensor is $w = 24\text{ mm}$ wide and the lens has $f = 12\text{ mm}$. What is the horizontal field of view?
Show solution
Step 1: half the view: $\tan\dfrac{\text{FOV}}{2} = \dfrac{w}{2f} = \dfrac{24}{24} = 1$, so the half-angle is $45^\circ$ [1]
Step 2: $\text{FOV} = 2 \times 45^\circ = 90^\circ$ [1]
Answer: $90^\circ$
007⭐⭐Choosing a focal length2 pts · ~4 min
A sensor is $36\text{ mm}$ wide. Which focal length gives a $120^\circ$ field of view? (Use $\tan 60^\circ \approx 1.73$.)
Show solution
Step 1: the half-angle is $60^\circ$, so $\dfrac{w}{2f} = \tan 60^\circ \approx 1.73$ [1]
Step 2: $f = \dfrac{w}{2 \times 1.73} = \dfrac{18}{1.73} \approx 10.4$
→ about 10 mm — a very wide-angle lens [1]
Answer: $f \approx 10.4\text{ mm}$
008⭐⭐⭐Dolly zoom3 pts · ~6 min
A camera with $f = 16\text{ mm}$ films a person $4\text{ m}$ away. A wall stands $40\text{ m}$ behind the person. The camera backs away until it is $10\text{ m}$ from the person. (a) Which focal length keeps the person the same size? (b) By how many times does the wall grow on the image?
Show solution
(a) Step 1: the person's size is $f \cdot X / Z$, so keep $f / Z$ fixed
    $\dfrac{f}{10} = \dfrac{16}{4} \;\Rightarrow\; f = 40\text{ mm}$ [1]
(b) Step 1: the wall's distance changes from $4 + 40 = 44\text{ m}$ to $10 + 40 = 50\text{ m}$. Its size goes with $f / Z$:
    before $\dfrac{16}{44} = \dfrac{4}{11}$, after $\dfrac{40}{50} = \dfrac{4}{5}$ [1]
Step 2: ratio $\dfrac{4/5}{4/11} = \dfrac{11}{5} = 2.2$
→ the wall looks 2.2 times bigger while the person stays the same [1]
Answer: (a) $f = 40\text{ mm}$ · (b) $\times 2.2$
009⭐Aperture: light and depth of field2 pts · ~3 min
A photographer changes the aperture from f/2.8 to f/5.6 (same lens, same focus). (a) What happens to the light reaching the sensor? (b) What happens to the depth of field?
Show solution
(a) Step 1: the opening's width is $f/N$; going from $N = 2.8$ to $N = 5.6$ halves the width, so the area — and the light — falls to $\left(\tfrac12\right)^2 = \tfrac14$ [1]
(b) Step 1: the blur circle of an out-of-focus point shrinks with the opening (half as wide), so more of the scene looks sharp: more depth of field [1]
Answer: (a) $\tfrac14$ of the light · (b) depth of field increases

C · Sensors

Slides for this part →
010⭐Image size in bytes2 pts · ~3 min
(a) How many bytes does a $1920 \times 1080$ greyscale image take at 8 bits per pixel, before compression? (b) And in colour, with 3 numbers per pixel?
Show solution
(a) Step 1: one byte per pixel: $1920 \times 1080 = 2\,073\,600$ bytes ≈ 2.1 MB [1]
(b) Step 1: three bytes per pixel: $2\,073\,600 \times 3 = 6\,220\,800$ bytes ≈ 6.2 MB [1]
Answer: (a) ≈ 2.1 MB · (b) ≈ 6.2 MB
011⭐Bit depth and levels2 pts · ~2 min
(a) How many levels can a 12-bit sensor record? (b) What is the smallest number of bits that gives at least 1000 levels?
Show solution
(a) Step 1: $b$ bits give $2^b$ levels: $2^{12} = 4096$ [1]
(b) Step 1: $2^9 = 512 < 1000$ and $2^{10} = 1024 \ge 1000$, so 10 bits [1]
Answer: (a) 4096 · (b) 10 bits
012⭐⭐Shot noise3 pts · ~4 min
In dim light, a pixel expects $N = 400$ photons. (a) How large is the random variation (the noise)? (b) What is the signal-to-noise ratio? (c) How many photons are needed to double that ratio?
Show solution
(a) Step 1: photon counts vary by $\sqrt{N} = \sqrt{400} = 20$ [1]
(b) Step 1: $\text{SNR} = \dfrac{N}{\sqrt N} = \sqrt{N} = 20$ [1]
(c) Step 1: $\text{SNR} = \sqrt N = 40 \Rightarrow N = 1600$ — four times the light, e.g. a four-times-longer exposure [1]
Answer: (a) ±20 photons · (b) 20 · (c) 1600 photons
Common mistake: doubling $N$ to double the SNR — the SNR grows only with $\sqrt N$.
013⭐⭐Dynamic range2 pts · ~3 min
A scene's brightest part is 2000 times brighter than its darkest. Can (a) an 8-bit image and (b) a 12-bit image hold both ends without clipping? Count the darkest non-black level as 1.
Show solution
(a) Step 1: 8 bits run from 1 to 255 — a range of 255 : 1 < 2000 : 1, so one end must clip [1]
(b) Step 1: 12 bits run from 1 to 4095 — 4095 : 1 > 2000 : 1, so both ends fit [1]
Answer: (a) no · (b) yes
014⭐Resolution2 pts · ~2 min
A camera's image is $1000 \times 750$ pixels. A newer model doubles both the width and the height. (a) How many pixels does each image have? (b) How many times more numbers must be stored?
Show solution
(a) Step 1: $1000 \times 750 = 750\,000$ and $2000 \times 1500 = 3\,000\,000$ [1]
(b) Step 1: $\dfrac{3\,000\,000}{750\,000} = 4$ — doubling both sides gives four times the pixels [1]
Answer: (a) 750 000 and 3 000 000 · (b) $\times 4$

D · Colour

Slides for this part →
015⭐Bayer filter counts2 pts · ~3 min
A camera's Bayer sensor has $6000 \times 4000$ photosites. How many of them measure (a) green, (b) red, (c) blue?
Show solution
Step 1: $6000 \times 4000 = 24\,000\,000$ photosites; each $2 \times 2$ tile holds 1 R, 2 G, 1 B, so half are green [1]
    green $= 12\,000\,000$
Step 2: red and blue take a quarter each: $6\,000\,000$ red and $6\,000\,000$ blue [1]
Answer: (a) 12 000 000 · (b) 6 000 000 · (c) 6 000 000
016⭐How many colours2 pts · ~2 min
How many different colours can one pixel hold with (a) 6 bits per channel and (b) 10 bits per channel?
Show solution
(a) Step 1: each channel has $2^6 = 64$ levels; three channels multiply: $64^3 = 2^{18} = 262\,144$ [1]
(b) Step 1: $\left(2^{10}\right)^3 = 2^{30} = 1\,073\,741\,824$ — about a billion [1]
Answer: (a) 262 144 · (b) $2^{30} \approx 1.07$ billion
017⭐Mixing light1.5 pts · ~2 min
Name the colour of each pixel: (a) $(255, 0, 255)$ (b) $(0, 255, 255)$ (c) $(128, 128, 128)$.
Show solution
Step 1: light adds. Red + blue = magenta [0.5]
Step 2: green + blue = cyan [0.5]
Step 3: three equal values = a grey — halfway between black and white [0.5]
Answer: (a) magenta · (b) cyan · (c) mid grey
Common mistake: mixing like paint (red + green = brown) — these are amounts of light.
018⭐⭐Demosaicing by hand2 pts · ~4 min
A photosite under a red filter reads 180. Its four green neighbours (up, down, left, right) read 100, 110, 90 and 120; its four blue neighbours (the diagonals) read 40, 60, 50 and 50. Using the average of the neighbours, what $(R, G, B)$ does this pixel get?
Show solution
Step 1: green is the average of the four green neighbours: $\dfrac{100 + 110 + 90 + 120}{4} = \dfrac{420}{4} = 105$ [1]
Step 2: blue is the average of the four blue neighbours: $\dfrac{40 + 60 + 50 + 50}{4} = \dfrac{200}{4} = 50$; red is measured directly [1]
Answer: $(R, G, B) = (180, 105, 50)$
019⭐⭐Rotating hue1.5 pts · ~2 min
In HSV, pure red has hue $0^\circ$, pure green $120^\circ$ and pure blue $240^\circ$. Every hue in a photo is turned by $+120^\circ$. What do (a) red, (b) green and (c) blue become?
Show solution
Step 1: $0^\circ + 120^\circ = 120^\circ$ → green [0.5]
Step 2: $120^\circ + 120^\circ = 240^\circ$ → blue [0.5]
Step 3: $240^\circ + 120^\circ = 360^\circ = 0^\circ$ → red — hue goes round a circle [0.5]
Answer: (a) green · (b) blue · (c) red
